docs.title: mai documentation
docs.text:
mai is a compiled language for statistical computing, from Brendan McArdle's 2018 PhD thesis at the University of Auckland. It reads like R but compiles to bytecode for a fast virtual machine.

Page What's in it Getting started Build, run a script, use the REPL, split code across files Language guide Values, types, declarations, functions, control flow, vectors and arrays Differences from R What an R user trips over first, in one table Built-in functions Every built-in, grouped by purpose Performance Benchmarks against R, and how to reproduce them Internals How the compiler and VM fit together, and where each part lives in the thesis

Worked examples live in ../examples. Each .mai script has a matching .out file holding its exact output, and make check runs them all. So the examples are tested along with everything else.

docs.title: Built-in functions
docs.text: These are all the functions the run-time provides (src/rt/builtins.c, src/arith/builtins.c, src/rt/options.c). Anything else, such as mean, map or which.min, is ordinary mai code that you write or include.

docs.title: Arithmetic and comparison operators
docs.text: + - * / ^, unary - and !, & | (element-wise boolean), && ||, == != < <= > >=, and a:b (integer range). All are element-wise on vectors and arrays and recycle the shorter operand.

docs.title: Maths (element-wise)
docs.text: Function sqrt, exp, log sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2(y, x) round rounds to the nearest whole number, returns double is_na

docs.title: Reductions
docs.text: sum, prod, any, all.

docs.title: Construction and conversion
docs.text: Function vec(...) vector from the arguments, optionally named: vec(a = 1, b = 2) vector(etyp, len, val) vector of type etyp and length len, filled with val array(etyp, shape, val) array of type etyp with the given shape vector dbl(n), int(n), bool(n), list(n) zero-filled vectors (list holds objects) cat(x, y) concatenation as_double, as_int, as_bool element-wise conversion (as_int truncates) as_type(x, type(T)) convert to any type

docs.title: Structure
docs.text: Function length(x) number of elements shape(a), rank(a) dimensions and number of dimensions of an array names(x), names(x) = syms element names, as a vector of symbols dimnames(a), dimnames(a) = v per-dimension names of an array

docs.title: Types
docs.text: Function typeof(x) the type of a value ret_type(t), elt_type(t) return type of a function type; element type of a vector or array type common_type(a, b) the type both promote to: common_type(type(int), type(double)) is double subtype(a, b), compat(a, b) type relations, as used by the compiler

docs.title: Random numbers
docs.text: srand(seed), runif(n), rnorm(n) and rand(min, max) (a random int), all from MT19937-64.

docs.title: Data exchange
docs.text:
Function read_vec(file, type(T)) read a file of raw T elements (int as 32-bit, double as 64-bit IEEE, boolean as one byte, native byte order) into a vector(T) write_vec(x, file) write the elements of an int, double or boolean vector or array the same way, returning the count; arrays are written column-major

These are how rmai passes data between R and mai exactly. From R, writeBin(x, f, size = 8) and readBin(f, "double", n) speak the same format.

docs.title: Program and environment
docs.text:
Function print(x) print and return nil stop(message) raise an error assert(cond) raise an error unless cond is true source(file) compile a file and return it as a function rm('name') remove a global options(...) get or set compiler and printing options (see Getting started) rt_time() real, user and system seconds since an arbitrary origin gc_collect() run the garbage collector eq(x, y) identity of two objects equal(x, y) equality of contents hash(x) hash of a value

Keywords that look like functions: if, while, for, function, return, break, continue, type(...), include "file", and the declarations var, let, const and global.

docs.title: Differences from R
docs.text:
mai keeps much of R's syntax and changes the semantics that stop R from being compiled well (thesis section 1.1). This table is what R users hit first.

R mai Notes TRUE, FALSE true, false x <- 1 x = 1 there is no <-, <<- or -> c(1, 2, 3) vec(1, 2, 3) cat(a, b) concatenates vectors numeric(n), integer(n), logical(n) dbl(n), int(n), bool(n) vector(type(double), n, fill) for an explicit fill list(a, b) vec(a, b), or list(n) then assign list(n) makes n empty slots for (i in 1:n) for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 1) C-style only; the loop variable is local to the loop 7 / 2 is 3.5 7 / 2 is 3 int / int stays int; write 7 / 2.0 2^31 is a double 2 ^ 31 is NA int overflow gives NA; write 2.0 ^ 31 x %% y, x %/% y not available as.integer, as.numeric as_int, as_double, as_bool, as_type(x, type(T)) is.na(x) is_na(x) scalars are length-1 vectors scalars are distinct types typeof(1) is int, typeof(1:1) is vector(int) copy-on-modify call by reference a function that assigns into a vector argument changes the caller's vector assignment in a function makes a local assignment to an undeclared name sets a global declare locals with var or let lazy arguments, substitute() eager arguments no non-standard evaluation sum(x, na.rm = TRUE) no na.rm system.time(expr) rt_time() before and after set.seed(1) srand(1) the generator is MT19937-64, so streams differ from R's source("f.R") include "f.mai" or source("f.mai")() source() returns the compiled file as a function library(pkg) not available no packages, S3/S4 or data frames yet lapply, sapply, apply write a loop, or a small typed map see examples/02-functions.mai mean, var, colSums, which.min not built in a few lines of mai each; the thesis's closest-points example defines which.min and colsum this way errors give a non-zero exit in Rscript the process exits 0 check the output

docs.title: What carries over unchanged
docs.text:
• if/else and { } blocks as expressions; the last value is returned.
  • First-class functions and closures, with default and named arguments.
  • Element-wise, recycling arithmetic and comparison on vectors.
  • a:b ranges, 1-based indexing, x[i], m[i, j], m[, j], names.
  • NA propagation.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
mai builds on Linux with glibc. You need a C11 compiler, GNU Bison 3, GNU M4, GNU readline and the valgrind headers.

sudo apt-get install build-essential bison m4 libreadline-dev valgrind
git clone https://github.com/mai-lib/mai
cd mai
make build          # tuned for this machine (-march=native)
make check          # runs tests/ and examples/

make build CTUNE= builds a binary that isn't tied to your CPU model, which is what CI does. The executable is build/main; copy or symlink it anywhere you like, for example ln -s "$PWD/build/main" ~/bin/mai.

docs.title: Run a script
docs.text:
build/main examples/01-basics.mai

A script runs top to bottom. Output comes from print(), and the value of the script's final expression is printed at the end. That is why most example outputs end in <nil>: print() itself returns nil.

Errors are printed with the name of the function that raised them, for example stop: singular X matrix. The process still exits with status 0, so check the output rather than the exit code.

docs.title: The REPL
docs.text:
Run build/main with no arguments to get an interactive prompt (>, and + for continuation lines) with readline editing and history.

When the REPL starts it loads ~/.maininit if that file exists. Set the INITFILE environment variable to use a different file. That makes it a good place for helper functions you always want, such as mean or map.

docs.title: Splitting code across files
docs.text:
• include "file.mai" reads another file in place, at compile time. The path is relative to the current directory.
  • source("file.mai") compiles a file at run time and returns it as a function of no arguments, so source("file.mai")() runs it.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
options() returns the current settings, and options(name = value) changes them:

Option Default Effect opt_builtin true specialise calls to built-in functions opt_inline true inline small const functions opt_dce true dead code elimination opt_constfold true constant folding opt_dvn true redundancy elimination (dominator-based value numbering) dbg_dump_ir false print the IR and bytecode of each newly compiled function print_digits 6 significant digits when printing doubles print_line 76 line width for printing vectors print_max 200 maximum number of elements printed print_name_max 15 maximum width of printed names

An option takes effect for code compiled after the call. Code in the same file was compiled before the call ran, so use include or source() to see its effect, as in the IR dump example in Internals.

docs.title: Internals
docs.text:
Every top-level expression, included file and source()d file is compiled before it runs:

  1. Parse (thesis ch. 4): a Bison grammar (src/grammar.y) and a hand-written lexer (src/lexer.c) build an abstract syntax tree.
  2. SSA conversion (ch. 5 to 9): the tree becomes a graph of basic blocks, and the compiler resolves scopes, builds the dominator tree and puts the graph into static single assignment form.
  3. Optimisation (ch. 10 to 14): sparse conditional constant propagation recovers types and constants. Small const functions are inlined, and variables captured by closures are moved into heap cells. Redundant computations are then removed by dominator-based value numbering.
  4. Code generation (ch. 15 to 18): live-range analysis and linear-scan allocation assign frame locations, SSA form is destroyed, and bytecode is emitted.
  5. Execution (ch. 26): a directly threaded virtual machine runs the bytecode. It has specialised instructions for unboxed int and double scalars, and calls into the run-time library (ch. 19 to 25) for objects, types, calls, vectors and garbage collection.

docs.title: Seeing it work
docs.text:
Set dbg_dump_ir and compile something afterwards (here, via source()) to print the optimised IR and the bytecode of each function:

# sq.mai
const sq = function(double x) : double x * x
print(sq(3.0))

options(dbg_dump_ir = true)
source("sq.mai")()

The body of sq comes out as:

function 0.0 sq.mai : function (double x) : double
block 0. (0 - 3)
0.0: BIND (argbits) (nil) : int
0.1: BIND x (nil) : double
0.2: BUILTIN `*`@double (1, 1) : double
0.3: RETURN 2

0000  mul.d   0  -40 -40
000e  ret     0

Because x is declared double, the generic * became a single unboxed mul.d instruction. Turning the passes off one at a time (for example options(opt_inline = false)) is a good way to see what each contributes.

docs.title: Where the code lives
docs.text:
The .nw files are the thesis chapters, each holding prose and code together. src/ is the code extracted from them.

Thesis chapter Literate source Extracted code 1 Introduction intro.nw the examples src/*.src, src/*.R, src/*.py 2 Executable main.nw src/main.c 3 Compiler compiler.nw src/compiler.c 4 Parser parser.nw src/lexer.c, src/grammar.y, src/parser.c 5 Intermediate Representation ir.nw src/ir.c, src/ir.h 6 AST Conversion ir_convert.nw src/ir_convert.c 7 IR Preparation ir_pre.nw src/ir_pre.c, src/ir_closure.c 8 Dominator Tree ir_dom.nw src/ir_dom.c 9 SSA Form Construction ir_ssa.nw src/ir_ssa.c 10 Analysis and Optimisation opt.nw src/opt_sccp.c, src/opt_trans.c 11 Inline Expansion opt_inline.nw src/opt_inline.c 12 Cell Introduction opt_closure.nw src/opt_closure.c 13 Postpass opt_post.nw src/opt_post.c, src/opt_call.c 14 Value Numbering opt_dvn.nw src/opt_dvn.c 15 Code Generation gen_code.nw src/gen_code.c 16 Live Range Analysis gen_range.nw src/gen_range.c 17 Location Allocation gen_loc.nw src/gen_loc.c 18 SSA Form Destruction gen_unssa.nw src/gen_unssa.c 19 Runtime runtime.nw src/rt/runtime.c 20 Types type.nw src/rt/type.c 21 Functions, Closures, Builtins callable.nw src/rt/callable.c 22 Calling Convention call.nw src/rt/call.c 23 Scalars scalar.nw src/rt/scalar.c 24 Vectors and Arrays vector.nw src/rt/vector.c 25 Memory Management gc.nw src/rt/gc.c 26 Virtual Machine vm.nw src/vm/ Appendices rt.nw, arith.nw, hash.nw, util.nw, debug.nw built-ins, options, maths library and RNG in src/rt/; M4-generated arithmetic kernels in src/arith/; hash tables and utilities

docs.title: Changing the code
docs.text: Edits to src/ are lost if src/ is ever regenerated from the .nw files. The project hasn't yet chosen whether src/ or the .nw files are the source of truth for new work. Until it does, make small fixes in src/ and mention them in the commit message.

docs.title: Language guide
docs.text: This is a practical tour of mai. Every snippet here has been run against the current build. The thesis remains the authoritative reference: chapter 4 covers the grammar, and chapters 19 to 25 cover the run-time library.

docs.title: Lexical basics
docs.text:
• Comments run from # to the end of the line.
  • Statements end at a newline or ;. Inside an open (, [ or { a newline continues the expression.
  • Identifiers may contain . and _, as in R (fib.arith, as_int). Wrap any other name in backticks.
  • Literals:
Literal Type 42 int 42.0, 1e-7, Inf double (Inf prints as inf) true, false boolean NA the missing value (it adopts the type it is used as) "text" string 'name' symbol type(double), type(vector(int)) type nil the null object

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text:
Scalars (int, double, boolean) are machine values, not length-one vectors, and each has its own missing value NA. Everything else is an object with reference semantics: strings, symbols, vectors, arrays, lists and functions.

print(typeof(1))        # int
print(typeof(1.0))      # double
print(typeof(1:3))      # vector(int)
print(typeof(function(double x) : double x))   # function (double x) : double

Arithmetic keeps the type of its operands. int with int gives int, so 7 / 2 is 3, and an int result that overflows becomes NA (2 ^ 31). Mixing in a double promotes to double: 7 / 2.0 is 3.5.

Type names: boolean, int, double, string, symbol, object, vector, vector(T), array, array(T), list, function and type. numeric stands for vector(double).

docs.title: Variables and declarations
docs.text:
Assignment uses = (there is no <-). Variables are either global or declared local. An assignment to a name that has not been declared as a local, even inside a function, creates or updates a global:

f = function() { y = 5; y }
f()
print(y)                    # 5: y leaked out as a global

So declare locals with var or let:

Form Meaning var x = 1, y = 2 local variables, scoped to the function let x = 1 local variable, scoped to the enclosing block const f = function(x) ... a global that can never be reassigned, so the compiler may inline it global xs, ys declare globals without giving them a value yet int i = 1, double s = 0.0 a typed declaration (also allowed after var and let) 
const limit = 10
f = function() {
    var total = 0
    for(int i = 1; i <= limit; i = i + 1)
        total = total + i
    total
}
print(f())              # 55

Reassigning a const is a compile-time error: invalid assignment to 'const k'. Scoping is strictly lexical: there is no assign(), get() or <<-, and a local is only visible in the block of code that declares it.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
area = function(w, h = 1) w * h
print(area(3))              # 3
print(area(h = 10, w = 2))  # 20
  • Arguments are matched by name, then by position, and defaults may refer to earlier arguments.
  • Arguments are evaluated before the call (no lazy evaluation, so no substitute() and no non-standard evaluation).
  • A formal can carry a type, function(double a, double b), and the function can declare a return type after the formals: function(x) : double .... Arguments are converted to declared scalar types: passing 2.5 to an int formal gives 2.
  • return(x) (or return x) leaves early; otherwise the value of the last expression is returned.
  • Functions are closures and capture their defining environment:
make_counter = function() {
    var n = 0
    function() { n = n + 1; n }
}
tick = make_counter()
tick(); tick()
print(tick())               # 3

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text:
if(x > 0) "positive" else "non-positive"     # if is an expression

while(i < 10) i = i + 1

for(int i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 1) {          # C-style for
    if(i == 4) break
    if(i == 2) continue
}

A loop variable declared in for(...) is local to the loop. Use while, or declare the variable beforehand, if you need its final value.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text:
v = 1:10                    # integer range
w = vec(1.5, 2.5, 3.5)      # vec() builds a vector from its arguments
named = vec(a = 1, b = 2)   # with names
z = dbl(3)                  # zero-filled: dbl(n), int(n), bool(n), list(n)
u = vector(type(double), 3, 1.5)   # explicit type, length and fill
both = cat(1:3, 4:5)        # concatenation
  • Indexing is 1-based: v[3], v[2:4]. v[] = 0 fills every element.
  • Arithmetic, comparison and maths functions work element-wise, recycling the shorter operand as in R: 1:6 * 1:2.
  • names(x) returns a vector of symbols, and names(x) = vec('a', 'b') sets them.
  • list(n) makes a vector of n objects, which can hold anything.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays are column-major, with a shape vector:

m = array(type(double), vec(2, 3), 0.0)
m[1, 2] = 5.0
m[, 3] = 7.0                # whole column
print(shape(m))             # 2 3
print(rank(m))              # 2
col = m[, 2]                # a column, as a vector

dimnames(m) and dimnames(m) = ... get and set the names of each dimension (nil when unset).

docs.title: Reference semantics
docs.text:
Vectors and arrays are passed by reference, not copied. A function that assigns into an argument changes the caller's data:

zero_first = function(v) { v[1] = 0; nil }
x = 1:5
zero_first(x)
print(x)                    # 0 2 3 4 5

When you need the original, pass a copy. Arithmetic always creates a new vector, so 1 * y or 1.0 * y is the quickest way to copy. Scalars are values, so reassigning a scalar argument never affects the caller.

docs.title: Missing values
docs.text: NA exists for each scalar type. It propagates through arithmetic (sum(vec(1.0, NA)) is NA) and is_na(x) tests for it. Unlike R, there is no na.rm argument.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: stop("message") raises an error. assert(cond) raises one if cond is false. An error aborts the current top-level expression and is printed as function: message.

docs.title: Randomness and timing
docs.text: srand(seed) seeds the generator, a 64-bit Mersenne Twister. runif(n), rnorm(n) and rand(min, max) draw from it. rt_time() returns a double vector of real, user and system seconds, so (rt_time() - t0)[1] is the elapsed wall time.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text: The thesis's motivating example is a least-squares fit by modified Gram-Schmidt. It is in examples/07-regression.mai and benchmarked against R in Performance.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
The thesis's aim is that ordinary loop-heavy code, the kind R users are taught to avoid, runs fast without being rewritten in C or vectorised.

Benchmark mai (s) R (s) Speedup Gram-Schmidt regression, n = 10000, k = 100 (thesis 1.2.1) 0.38 1.35 3.5x Nearest neighbour by double loop, 500 x 500 points in 100-d (thesis 1.2.2) 0.35 0.92 2.6x Scalar loop, sum of 1/i for 1e7 steps 0.13 0.32 2.5x Recursive calls, fib(27) 0.08 0.20 2.5x Vectorised sum(sqrt(x * x + 1)), 5e6 elements 0.10 0.05 0.5x

These are medians of 5 runs after a warm-up, on one core of an Intel Xeon at 2.8 GHz, with mai built with make build CTUNE= and R 4.3.3 (which byte-compiles functions by default).

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
• Loops, calls and scalar arithmetic are where mai wins. Type recovery lets the compiler emit unboxed double and int instructions, and small const helpers like dotprod are inlined.
  • Long vectorised expressions are where R wins. Each of R's built-ins is a tight C loop, while mai evaluates x * x + 1 as separate whole-vector operations through its VM. Stream fusion of vector expressions is on the thesis's future-work list (section 1.4).
  • Timings for the thesis's own machine (an AMD FX-8350) are in section 1.2: 0.53 s for mai against 1.36 s for R 3.5.3 on the regression, a similar ratio to the one above.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
Each benchmark is a pair of files in ../bench, name.mai and name.R, and each defines run().

make build CTUNE=
bench/run.sh build/main 5           # writes bench/results.csv
Rscript bench/plot.R                # writes docs/images/benchmarks.png

To add a benchmark, drop in a new name.mai and name.R pair that each define run(), and give it a label in bench/plot.R.
